Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is the enzyme that catalyses the reaction of an Acyl-CoA molecule with carnitine to form Acylcarnitine.  CAT I is located on the outer mitochondrial membrane, and once Acylcarnitine has been transported across the mitochondrial membrane, Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT II) catalyses the reaction of Acylcarnitine with carnitine to form Acyl-CoA and carnitine. CAT II is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane, and Acyl-CoA is then able to enter the mitochondrial matrix to be used in beta-oxidation.

The answer is spinal stenosis. This is where there is narrowing of the spinal canal, usually due to age related scalency of the vertebrae. This can lead to compression of the nerves of the lumbar or even sacral regions.  Features of the history that suggest spinal stenosis are:» Older patient (65)» Pain in lower back and legs (often bilateral in stenosis, radiculopathy is more unilaateral)» Worse on walking (claudication) – worse especially on going downhill – flexion increases the diameter of the spinal canal and sacral hiatus, opening up the region to compression therefore worse on downhill when going into flexion » Tingling in legs is common in stenosis (LMC may also be affected)» Relieved by rest and sitting in a chair or crouching – flexion relieves the compression again whereas in prolapsed disc flexion increases diameter of canal and relieves compression therefore spinal nerves are decompressed  Straight leg raise test is negative as this is not a prolapsed disc  N/B: Dog leg sign would be present if it was a prolapsed IV disc
